theory.title: Node.js Architecture & Event Loop
theory.content:
How Node.js Works

Node.js is a single-threaded, event-driven runtime built on V8. It handles I/O operations (network, file system) asynchronously via the libuv library, which manages a thread pool for blocking operations under the hood.

Event Loop Phases

  1. timers — executes setTimeout and setInterval callbacks
  2. pending callbacks — I/O error callbacks from previous iteration
  3. idle, prepare — internal Node use
  4. poll — retrieve new I/O events; execute their callbacks
  5. check — setImmediate callbacks
  6. close callbacks — socket/handle close events
console.log('1 — sync');

setTimeout(() => console.log('4 — timer'), 0);
setImmediate(() => console.log('3 — immediate'));

Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('2 — microtask'));

// Output: 1 → 2 → 3 → 4
// (microtasks run before each phase; setImmediate before setTimeout in I/O context)

Why Non-Blocking Matters

Because Node is single-threaded, a CPU-intensive synchronous operation blocks ALL requests. Use worker_threads for CPU-heavy work; keep the main thread free for I/O.

theory.title: Streams & Buffers
theory.content:
Why Streams?

Streams let you process data incrementally as it arrives, rather than loading everything into memory. Essential for large files, HTTP responses, or real-time data.

Stream Types

  • Readable — source of data (fs.createReadStream, HTTP request body)
  • Writable — destination (fs.createWriteStream, HTTP response)
  • Duplex — both readable and writable (TCP socket)
  • Transform — duplex that modifies data (gzip, encryption)
const { createReadStream, createWriteStream } = require('fs');
const { createGzip } = require('zlib');

// Compress a file using streams — handles any file size with ~64KB RAM
createReadStream('input.log')
  .pipe(createGzip())
  .pipe(createWriteStream('input.log.gz'))
  .on('finish', () => console.log('Done'));

Async Iteration (Modern API)

async function processLines(filePath) {
  const stream = createReadStream(filePath, { encoding: 'utf8' });
  for await (const chunk of stream) {
    // process each chunk without loading whole file
    console.log(chunk.length, 'bytes');
  }
}

Buffers

Buffer is a fixed-size chunk of raw binary memory. Used when working with TCP streams, file I/O, and binary protocols.

const buf = Buffer.from('Hello', 'utf8');
buf.toString('hex');    // '48656c6c6f'
buf.toString('base64'); // 'SGVsbG8='

theory.title: Module Systems
theory.content:
CommonJS (CJS)

The original Node.js module system. Modules are loaded synchronously with require(). The module cache means repeated require() calls return the same instance.

// utils.js
const { format } = require('date-fns');

function formatDate(date) {
  return format(date, 'yyyy-MM-dd');
}

module.exports = { formatDate };
// or individual: exports.formatDate = formatDate;

// index.js
const { formatDate } = require('./utils');
const path = require('path'); // built-in
const express = require('express'); // node_modules

ES Modules (ESM)

Modern, standardised module system. Statically analysed, enabling tree-shaking. Enable with "type": "module" in package.json or .mjs extension.

// utils.mjs
export function formatDate(date) { ... }
export const VERSION = '1.0';
export default class DateHelper { ... }

// index.mjs
import DateHelper, { formatDate, VERSION } from './utils.mjs';
import { readFile } from 'node:fs/promises'; // node: prefix for built-ins (ESM best practice)

// Dynamic import (works in both CJS and ESM)
const module = await import('./heavy-module.mjs');

Interoperability

  • CJS can require() a CJS module or use createRequire to load CJS from ESM
  • ESM can import a CJS module (default export becomes module.exports)
  • ESM cannot be synchronously require()-d from CJS without a wrapper

theory.title: Built-in Modules
theory.content:
fs — File System

const fs = require('node:fs/promises'); // Promise-based API

const content = await fs.readFile('./data.json', 'utf8');
const data = JSON.parse(content);

await fs.writeFile('./out.json', JSON.stringify(data, null, 2));
await fs.mkdir('./output', { recursive: true });
const files = await fs.readdir('./src');

path — Path Utilities

const path = require('node:path');

path.join('src', 'utils', 'date.js');   // 'src/utils/date.js' (cross-platform)
path.resolve('../config.json');          // absolute path from cwd
path.dirname('/foo/bar/file.js');        // '/foo/bar'
path.extname('report.pdf');              // '.pdf'
path.basename('/foo/bar/file.js', '.js'); // 'file'

// ESM equivalent of __dirname
import { fileURLToPath } from 'node:url';
const __dirname = path.dirname(fileURLToPath(import.meta.url));

http/https — HTTP Server

const http = require('node:http');

const server = http.createServer((req, res) => {
  if (req.url === '/health') {
    res.writeHead(200, { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' });
    res.end(JSON.stringify({ status: 'ok' }));
  } else {
    res.writeHead(404);
    res.end('Not Found');
  }
});

server.listen(3000, () => console.log('Listening on :3000'));

events — EventEmitter

const { EventEmitter } = require('node:events');

class Queue extends EventEmitter {
  #items = [];
  enqueue(item) {
    this.#items.push(item);
    this.emit('item', item);
  }
}

const q = new Queue();
q.on('item', item => console.log('Received:', item));
q.enqueue('task-1');

theory.title: Express.js Basics
theory.content:
Setting Up an Express App

import express from 'express';
import cors from 'cors';

const app = express();

app.use(cors());
app.use(express.json()); // parse JSON request bodies

// Routes
app.get('/api/users', async (req, res) => {
  const users = await db.user.findMany();
  res.json(users);
});

app.post('/api/users', async (req, res) => {
  const { name, email } = req.body;
  const user = await db.user.create({ data: { name, email } });
  res.status(201).json(user);
});

app.listen(3000);

Middleware

Middleware functions have access to req, res, and next. They run in order for every matching request.

// Logging middleware
app.use((req, res, next) => {
  console.log(`${req.method} ${req.url}`);
  next(); // pass to next handler
});

// Auth middleware
function requireAuth(req, res, next) {
  const token = req.headers.authorization?.split(' ')[1];
  if (!token) return res.status(401).json({ error: 'Unauthorised' });
  req.user = verifyToken(token);
  next();
}

app.get('/api/profile', requireAuth, (req, res) => {
  res.json(req.user);
});

Error Handling

// 4-argument signature = error handler
app.use((err, req, res, next) => {
  console.error(err.stack);
  const status = err.status ?? 500;
  res.status(status).json({ error: err.message });
});

theory.title: Error Handling
theory.content:
Synchronous Errors

// Always use try/catch for sync throws
function parseConfig(json) {
  try {
    return JSON.parse(json);
  } catch (err) {
    throw new Error(`Invalid config: ${err.message}`);
  }
}

Async/Await Error Handling

// Unhandled promise rejections crash Node 15+
process.on('unhandledRejection', (reason, promise) => {
  console.error('Unhandled rejection:', reason);
  process.exit(1);
});

// Wrap async route handlers
const asyncHandler = fn => (req, res, next) =>
  Promise.resolve(fn(req, res, next)).catch(next);

app.get('/users', asyncHandler(async (req, res) => {
  const users = await db.user.findMany();
  res.json(users);
}));

Custom Error Classes

class AppError extends Error {
  constructor(message, public status = 500) {
    super(message);
    this.name = 'AppError';
  }
}

class NotFoundError extends AppError {
  constructor(resource) {
    super(`${resource} not found`, 404);
  }
}

// Usage
if (!user) throw new NotFoundError('User');

Process-Level Handlers

  • process.on('uncaughtException') — last resort for synchronous throws
  • process.on('unhandledRejection') — unhandled Promise rejections
  • In production, log and exit gracefully; let a process manager restart

theory.title: Worker Threads & Cluster
theory.content:
Why Multi-Processing?

Node.js is single-threaded, so CPU-bound work (image processing, crypto, heavy computation) blocks the event loop. Two solutions: worker_threads (shared memory, same process) and cluster (multiple processes, separate memory).

Worker Threads

// main.js
const { Worker } = require('node:worker_threads');

function runWorker(data) {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    const worker = new Worker('./heavy-task.js', { workerData: data });
    worker.on('message', resolve);
    worker.on('error', reject);
  });
}

const result = await runWorker({ size: 1000000 });

// heavy-task.js
const { workerData, parentPort } = require('node:worker_threads');
const result = performHeavyComputation(workerData);
parentPort.postMessage(result);

Cluster Module

const cluster = require('node:cluster');
const os = require('node:os');

if (cluster.isPrimary) {
  const cpus = os.availableParallelism();
  for (let i = 0; i < cpus; i++) cluster.fork();
  cluster.on('exit', (worker) => {
    console.log(`Worker ${worker.process.pid} died, restarting`);
    cluster.fork();
  });
} else {
  // Each worker runs the HTTP server
  require('./server');
}

When to Use Each

  • Worker Threads — CPU-intensive work with shared data (SharedArrayBuffer)
  • Cluster — scale HTTP servers across all CPU cores
  • child_process.spawn/exec — run external programs or shell commands
